text: Well, first of all, hi, everyone.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm an engineer on the product growth team at Notion and now working on the GTM engineering team.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A year ago, I would have told you that building a GTM system was a marketing ops problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And today, I think it's one of the most interesting distributed systems problems that I've worked on.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: GTM at most companies involve a spider web of tools like what you see here, and they're stitched together by customer notes, proposals, contracts that are passed back and forth.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Over the last few months, a small team and myself, we've been trying to turn this spider web into a unified GTM system.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We're still in the midst of it, but we've learned a ton that I'd like to share with you today.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this isn't really a new problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We've been wrestling with pieces of it for years, lifecycle messaging, product recommendations, sales automations, customer data, and onboarding.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But the solutions were fragmented because the underlying technology forced them to be.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then over the winter break, our CEO Ivan spent it building a video game, and he came back convinced that software engineering could be applied to many problems that were previously unwieldy or too costly.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: At the same time, our ability to execute skyrocketed with agentic technology, and the breadth of problems we could solve did too.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The costly, time-consuming, and previously unsolvable spaghetti could now be sorted.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what we found is that GTM had become a systems problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That made us realize we could chip away at this holistically.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In case you don't know, Notion's platform is a collaborative brain for human and agents to think together.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Over the years, we've evolved into a context layer for your company, and AI agents can act on it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Notion's business moves between self-serve growth and sales assist, and customers move between these two motions all the time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The problem is that customers experience one journey, but internally it is supported by disconnected systems that don't actually talk to each other very well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: These processes were rife with human error and put a lot of cognitive burden on our teams.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For example, sales reps are probably not the strongest at managing systems, but their strength is in sussing out human signals during the buying process.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So every time they had to context switch between after a call, doing research, drafting follow-up, they were spending less time with our customers and customer problems.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Most companies have separate systems for sales assist and product-led growth, and this is actually also true for us.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Marketing runs on one set of tools, sales on another, customer ops on a third, but all of them are looking at a customer independently and making decisions separately.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what we set out to build is a single decisioning system that spans self-serve growth and sales assist, and it can help the customer decide the next step so that everything is cohesive.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Our vision is for this system to be programmable, proactive, and continuous.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When we started, we were faced with some challenges.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There was no single source of truth, so customer data was spread across Salesforce, Gong, Outreach, Zoom Info, and many more.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Product usage lived in Snowflake.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And a decade of the most important context lived in Notes and Meeting Docs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Yes, our sales reps do use Notion for that, too.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Notion employees were actively using MCPs and their own agents to solve problems already, but they were innovating within their own departments.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So it was single player mode, or you could say here, single department mode.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Marketing built tools for marketing, sales built tools for sales, and each tool served a tiny slice of that customer journey, and it would make it really hard to create something that was more holistic.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When we tried to automate across all of that, we hit some roadblocks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First, data quality.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Conflicting systems of records, wrong contacts tied to different accounts.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One bad mapping was enough to lose trust for sales rep. Secondly, data latency.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Every vendor added a hop, and this lag was causing us to act on stale data, and that meant we were automating on yesterday's world.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Third, and this is a big one, structured and unstructured data.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The most important facts about a customer were left in notes, like the champion just left, or don't contact this customer again, or they're blocked and legal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so these are exactly the types of notes that help sales rep move forward and decide what to do next.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And if an automation couldn't see it or process it, it could do something catastrophically wrong.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So our project team consisted of CX, RevOps, product, engineering, sales.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And after brainstorming together, we all kept finding the same patterns underneath that complexity.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Whoops, oh.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Every workflow could be reduced to four questions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What do we know about the customer?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What should happen next?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: How do we execute that safely?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And did it work?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That became our architecture.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the system has four layers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Know, a context layer we can trust about every customer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Decide, choose the single next best step for them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Third, act and fire a concrete action that could be a lifecycle email, an in-app nudge, or a task handed to a rep. And then learn, watch what happened and feed it back into the decisioning so that it's a loop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But this architecture is missing something important.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The most important part is that humans and agents are operating on the same loop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Concretely, this means that the context needs to be displayed so that humans and agents can read and operate on it together.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you can see that they're working in the same system, but they might have different roles.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Agents do the repetitive work at scale, like gathering context, researching, drafting recommendations, and writing artifacts.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Humans provide the judgment, adding nuance, deciding what to do next and if a recommendation is correct, and owning the customer relationship.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We found that instead of building an AI layer on top of our business, we designed our architecture so that the agent can operate as another operator within the same system as humans.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Before we built the system, we made some choices about how we were going to implement this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Firstly, we deliberately chose not to let an agent talk directly to a customer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For sales assist workflows, humans stay in the loop by default and approve anything the agents do.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The agents do the busy work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That decision also has a security dimension too.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If a prospect fills out a contact sales form online, we treat that as untrusted user input.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so trust boundaries don't break down, especially because there is an agent in the middle.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Secondly, routing and eligibility became a first-class primitive.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Eligibility used to be scattered all over the place.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We had one checker rule in an email tool, another in sales, and we pulled that all into one place so that these rules can be consumed across our code base, product, sales, engineering, and these are like customer segmentations or signal definitions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then a single classifier will route what the customer should do.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this will actually prevent double sends from our system and create very cohesive communication across.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And last but not least, we decided that it was very important to own the context layer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we decided to rent everything else.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Since we are a lean team, we will not build our own email vendor or enrichment services like Clay.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We use Clay.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we believe that we understood our customers the best.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we will not give that away.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So let's get into what we built.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The first step was to gather a consolidated view of all of our customers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Snowflake, which is our data warehouse, is where we compute this truth.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We ingest data from all the vendors in our GTM stack to Snowflake.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We run daily transforms, and in some cases, real time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: To produce a small set of modeled versioned entities.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And these are accounts, contacts, workspaces, eligibility and facts.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this also has clear ownership of what teams or tools they come from and like timestamps.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: DynamoDB is our key value store and it's where we compute our truth or serve our truth.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We publish a denormalized key addressable profile that agents can quickly query in milliseconds with no joins.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We also persist agent-persisted or generated artifacts.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And these are research snippets, summarized notes, rolling summaries.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And these unstructured data are also keyed by the same IDs so that downstream systems can read all of this in one shot.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this data was normalized, and of course we brought it into Notion so that we could work with structured and unstructured data at the same time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So some of the data I showed you in the boxes earlier, there's product usage data, there's activity log from across our vendor stack, and then we also have unstructured data, like I mentioned, that is most important for sales context with research reports and notes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this turned out to be powerful for two reasons.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First, our internal GTM teams didn't need to jump between many tools anymore.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They could use Notion itself, a tool they were already using, to explore context, investigate accounts, answer questions, and they could even take actions like sending to Nooks or sending to Outreach.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is a tool that they were very familiar with, and they didn't need to open seven tabs anymore.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Secondly, because we weren't building an AI layer, humans, workflows, and agents could all operate on the same source of truth.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In a very literal sense, we are using Notion to grow Notion.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The next primitive we decided that we needed was a way to turn customer events into actions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The unit here is a signal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A signal is a single customer event that's important enough to change what should happen next for a customer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Some are user-driven, like a customer hitting their AI limit, or maybe they reached out to contact sales.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But some of them are not user-initiated at all, which are these external signal examples I listed here, like company raising funding, hiring signals, or shift in their tech stack.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Those external signals are what allowed us to be proactive instead of reactive.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is the signal service that watches the customer profile, decides whether a single action is available, decides who should own that action, and then it emits a concrete task following the architecture I described before.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this task could be for a human or an agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If there is a task for a sales rep, that actually just lands in their Notion database, and they can quickly view it and act on it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What's interesting about the way we built our GTM systems is that if there is no signal about a customer, the marketing component of our system kicks in.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We have a predictive engine that will recommend product features most relevant for that customer, and it will send out lifecycle emails and in-app nudges or multi-channel communication to drive a customer towards adoption automatically.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So diving deep into a small slice of what happens when we decide what action should be emitted, this is for the sales workflow.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we shadowed our best reps to capture something that was the most repetitive part of our job and encoded it as a durable multi-agent workflow.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Every signal becomes a workflow on Temporal, which is something we rent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And a single run will touch enrichment, web search, draft generation, and more.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Each of these is a network call that could fail or rate limit.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so Temporal lets us focus on writing the sequential logic for our GTM use cases while it will handle the retries, dedupes, and handling and going back to exactly where failures left off.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And one malformed transcript can't take down the whole batch, which was really important to us.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So an example of a cold outbound signal for us, we'll have a research sub-agent do concurrent web researches.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then I'll draft like an email.

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then a review agent will pick the highest scoring one and make any updates if necessary.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this also operates on a loop so that the email drafts are improved.

text: And then when it's ready, this email draft will land in the sales task that is available for them to act on.

text: For more reactive signals after a follow-up call,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The Gong transcript will come in, our agent will parse the transcript, and then, again, it will extract the critical sales med pick data, metrics, economic buyer, decision criteria, plan, and champion, and draft a grounded follow-up for that.

text: The third layer is what turns this automation into a system that self-improves.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Every action is a decision log and every outcome threads back to the decision that caused it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the naive version of this is a data analyst coming in and trying to understand if the output of this could be better.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So one of the questions that we came across along every step of the way is a classic question, do we build or buy?

speaker: SPEAKER_00
